cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Hi Coleman, how are you?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: Good, thanks.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: I wanted to have a chat with you because our friend Josh told me that you’ve joined a guitar group and it sounds interesting. I’d really like to learn myself.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: Why don’t you come along? I’m sure there’s room for another person.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Really? So – who runs the classes?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: He’s called a ‘coordinator’ – his name’s Gary Mathieson. Q1

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Let me note that down. Gary. . . . How do you spell his surname?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: It’s M-A-T-H-I-E-S-O-N.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Right, thanks.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: He’s retired, actually, but he’s a really nice guy and he used to play in a lot of bands.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Thanks. So how long have you been going?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: About a month now.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: And could you play anything before you started?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: I knew a few chords, but that’s all.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: I’m sure everyone will be better than me.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: That’s what I thought, too. When I first spoke to Gary on the phone, he said it was a class for beginners, but I was still worried that everyone would be better than me, but we were all equally hopeless! Q2

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Oh, that’s reassuring. So where do you meet?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: Well, when I joined the group, they were meeting in Gary’s home, but as the group got bigger, he decided to book a room at the college in town. I prefer going there. Q3

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: I know that place. I used to go to tap dancing classes there when I was at secondary school. I haven’t been since, though and I can’t remember what road it’s in… is it Lock Street?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: It’s just beyond there at the bottom of New Street near the city roundabout. Q4

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Yes, of course.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: The guitar club is on the first floor in Room T347.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Right. And when do you meet? Is it at the weekend?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: We meet on Thursdays. It used to be 10.30 and that suited me well, but now we meet at 11. The class that’s in there before us asked if they could have the room for another 30 minutes. Q5

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Oh, I see. Well, I’d love to come, but I don’t have a guitar.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: Well, you can always buy a second-hand one. There’s a website called ‘The perfect instrument’ that sells all kinds of guitars, violins and so on. I’m sure you’ll find something there. Q6

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: So what’s a typical lesson like with Gary?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: Well, he always starts by getting us to tune our guitars. That takes about five minutes.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Uhuh.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: Some people have an app they use, but others do it by ear. Gary goes round and helps them. And while he’s doing that, he tells us what he’s going to do during the lesson. Q7

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Right.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: First, we usually spend about ten minutes doing some strumming.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: So is that using . . . what are they called . . . plectrums?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: No – we just use our thumbs.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Much easier.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: Gary reminds us where to put our fingers for each chord and then we play them together. Sometimes we all just start laughing because we’re so bad at keeping time, so Gary starts clapping to help us. Q8

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Do you learn to play any songs?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: Yes – we do at least one song with words and chords. I mean that’s harder than you think.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Oh, I’m sure it is!

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: That part of the lesson takes about 15 minutes. He often brings a recording of the song and plays it to us first. Then he hands out the song and if there’s a new chord in it, we practise that before we play it together – but really slowly. Q9

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Do you do any finger picking?

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: That’s the last ten minutes of the lesson, when we pick out the individual notes from a tune he’s made up. It’s always quite simple.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: That must be hard, though.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: It is, but people like it because they can really concentrate and if we’re all playing well, it sounds quite impressive. The only trouble is that he sometimes gets us to play one at a time – you know, alone. Q10

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: That’s scary.

cues.speaker: COLEMAN
cues.text: It is, but I’ve got used to it now. At the end he spends about five minutes telling us what to practise for the following week.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Well, thanks Coleman. I’ll go and have a look at that website, I think.
